screens.title: Leveraging AWS Global Infrastructure for Performance
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how to make global applications faster and more resilient by leveraging AWS's physical footprint: Regions, Availability Zones, and hundreds of Edge Locations. We'll link these building blocks to two services that optimize network performance: Amazon CloudFront for content delivery and AWS Global Accelerator for dynamic application traffic. You'll see why placing resources near users matters, how caching reduces origin load, and when Anycast IPs over the AWS backbone give consistently lower latency than the public internet. I will also show a practical pattern: CloudFront at the edge for static assets, and Global Accelerator for interactive A P I or session traffic. As we progress we'll examine a hands-on CloudFront configuration for an S3 static website so you can observe cache hits and misses. By the end you'll be able to pick the right service for images, APIs, or real-time streams and design a layered architecture that balances cost, performance, and resilience. Consider which part of your application most affects user experience: assets or interactive calls?

Leveraging AWS Global Infrastructure for Performance

Learn how Regions, AZs, and Edge Locations work with CloudFront and Global Accelerator to reduce latency and improve availability for global users.

Regions & AZs
Placement and resilience for compute and storage.
Edge Locations
Cache and accelerate delivery near users.
CloudFront & Global Accelerator
Choose the right tool for static vs dynamic traffic.
Explore Key Topics
Edge caching, Anycast routing, and layered design patterns to give users fast, reliable access wherever they are.
Layered performance
Edge + Backbone + Regional endpoints
Example:
Use CloudFront to cache images, CSS, and video segments at Edge Locations while routing API calls through Global Accelerator to regional load balancers for consistent, low-latency sessions.
Coming up
We'll review core definitions, compare services, design a layered architecture, and walk through a CloudFront + S3 activity you can try yourself.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide our lesson so you can apply AWS global infrastructure effectively. First, you will explain how Regions, Availability Zones, and Edge Locations affect latency and resilience; knowing this helps you place compute and storage close to users and reduces single points of failure. Second, you will describe AWS Global Accelerator: how it uses static Anycast IPs and the AWS backbone to route interactive traffic with lower variability than the public internet. Third, you will understand how Amazon CloudFront caches static and semi-dynamic content at Edge Locations to speed delivery and reduce origin load. Fourth, you will learn to choose between CloudFront and Global Accelerator and to design a basic layered global architecture combining both when appropriate. Each objective includes a short competency milestone so you can verify understanding by explaining a real architecture choice. Together these skills let you improve user experience for static content, A P I calls, and real-time sessions, and form the foundation for rigorous performance testing across geographies.

screens.title: AWS Regions and Availability Zones
screens.narratorSegment: Start with the foundation: Regions and Availability Zones. A Region is a geographic area that contains multiple Availability Zones. An AZ is one or more discrete data centers with independent power, cooling, and networking, connected by low-latency links. Together, these define where your compute and storage run. The important performance rule is proximity: placing resources closer to your users reduces round-trip time. The important resilience rule is distribution: spreading instances across multiple AZs ensures that an outage in one AZ usually won’t fully take down your service. A common misconception is that Regions are a single data center; they are not. Another misconception is that AZ distribution alone solves global latency—if your users are on another continent, AZ distribution within one Region won't fix long-haul latency. A concrete example: serving a European user from an EU Region reduces latency compared to a US Region. When you design, map where users are, choose Regions closest to concentrations of traffic, and deploy across AZs in that Region for high availability. Key takeaway: placement controls both latency and fault isolation, so plan Regions for geographic reach and AZs for regional resilience.

keyIdea.title: Definition summary
keyIdea.text: Regions provide geographic separation; AZs provide isolated failure domains. Use both to balance latency and availability.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Regions & AZs
What they are
A Region is a geographical area made of multiple Availability Zones. AZs are isolated data centers with redundant infrastructure connected by low-latency links.
Why it matters
  • Latency is proportional to distance; choose Regions near your users to minimize round-trip time.
  • Distribute across AZs to tolerate a single data center failure without losing the whole service.
  • AZs share low-latency connectivity, which supports synchronous replication and failover patterns.
Concrete example
An e-commerce site with customers in Europe deploys the storefront frontend and a replica of its database in an EU Region and spreads web servers across two AZs to avoid a single-AZ outage.
Key Takeaway

Regions determine geographic reach; AZs provide fault isolation inside a Region. Choose regions for reach, AZs for resilience.

Common mistake
Assuming AZ spread removes cross-continent latency. It doesn't—use regional placement to reduce long-haul delays.

screens.title: Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches
screens.narratorSegment: Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches are the components that bring content physically closer to users. Edge Locations are numerous points of presence that serve cached content directly to end users. Regional Edge Caches sit between origins and Edge Locations, holding popular content for larger regions to reduce origin fetch frequency. The practical effect is twofold: latency is reduced because content often travels only to a nearby edge, and origin load decreases because repeated requests are served from edge caches. A common misconception is that caching only helps truly static files; in reality caching policies and invalidation allow CloudFront to serve semi-dynamic content when appropriate. For example, product images, C S S, and library files benefit hugely from edge caching, while frequently changing personalized data often should bypass caches or use short TTLs. When setting cache policies, consider object type, freshness requirements, and cache-control headers. Key takeaway: Edge Locations speed delivery and Regional Edge Caches amplify cache effectiveness across a region, together reducing latency and origin pressure. Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches means edge locations immediately serve cached content to reduce latency; regional edge caches act as regional staging layers to lower origin requests.. In practical terms, how amazon places content close to users and why that reduces origin load. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Edge Locations
What Edge Locations do
Serve cached content from a nearby data center so the request does not traverse long distances to the origin.
Benefits:
  • Lower latency for end users.
  • Lower origin request rates and costs.
  • Edge-level protections, including mitigations against some volumetric attacks.
Regional Edge Caches
Act as regional mid-tier caches for less-frequently requested objects, reducing the need to fetch from the origin.
Practical note: Use caching and invalidation policies to control freshness—short TTLs for changing content, long TTLs for static assets.
Concrete example
A media site caches video segments at Edge Locations so playback starts quickly for viewers worldwide. A Regional Edge Cache keeps popular segments available for longer, reducing origin bandwidth spikes during viral events.

screens.title: How CloudFront Caches Content
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the request lifecycle for CloudFront so you can see how cache hits and misses affect latency and origin load. When a user requests an object, CloudFront first checks the nearest Edge Location. If the object is cached and valid, CloudFront returns it immediately — this is a cache hit and yields the lowest latency. If not cached, the request may be forwarded to a Regional Edge Cache; if it's present there, the response is returned and the Edge caches it for subsequent users. On a miss at both levels, CloudFront fetches the object from the origin, such as an S3 static website endpoint or an Application Load Balancer, and then caches it according to the distribution's cache policy. Important controls include Cache-Control headers, CloudFront cache policies, and invalidation requests which force removal of cached objects. A common misconception is that the first user always experiences the same latency as later users; in fact, the first request will often be slower due to origin fetch, while subsequent requests are faster because of cached copies. Takeaway: tune TTLs and origins to maximize hits for stable assets and plan for misses in load tests.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle insight
keyIdea.text: Edge Location -> Regional Edge Cache -> Origin. Cache hits give fastest responses; misses cause origin fetch and higher latency.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › CloudFront Cache Flow
Step-by-step
  1. User requests object; Edge Location checks cache.
  2. If miss, ask Regional Edge Cache; if still miss, fetch from origin.
  3. CloudFront caches object per policy and returns response.
  4. Subsequent requests hit the Edge and respond faster.
Controls that matter
Cache-Control headers, CloudFront cache policies, invalidation, and origin configuration.
Visual example
Imagine a user in Brazil requests an image. CloudFront checks the Sao Paulo edge. If cached, immediate response. If not, it checks a regional cache, then the origin in the appropriate Region. After the origin response, the edge caches the image for the next user in Brazil.
Key Takeaway
Design cache policies for object freshness and aim to maximize hits for stable assets to reduce latency and origin load.

screens.title: How AWS Global Accelerator Works
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Global Accelerator provides static Anycast IP addresses that act as fixed entry points for your users. When a client connects to one of these Anycast IPs, the connection is accepted at the nearest Edge Location. From there, Global Accelerator routes the traffic across the AWS backbone to the optimal healthy endpoint—this might be an Application Load Balancer or an EC2 instance in the best Region. The main benefit is consistent and often lower latency compared to routing over the public internet, because the majority of the path uses the optimized AWS network. A common misunderstanding is thinking Global Accelerator caches content; it does not. Instead, it optimizes transport for dynamic or interactive traffic where content changes frequently or sessions must persist. For instance, a multiplayer game uses Global Accelerator to direct a player to the nearest healthy game server with minimal jitter. When considering Global Accelerator, evaluate session patterns, whether static Anycast IPs simplify firewall rules, and whether your application gains from routing consistency. Key takeaway: Global Accelerator optimizes routing and availability—not caching—and is ideal for interactive, latency-sensitive workloads.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Global Accelerator
Key mechanics
  • Clients connect to static Anycast IPs.
  • Traffic enters the AWS network at the nearest Edge Location.
  • Global Accelerator routes to the best healthy endpoint across Regions.
Practical benefits
Lower variability in latency, predictable entry points for firewall and client configuration, and faster failover to healthy endpoints.
Concrete example
A multiplayer game uses Global Accelerator so players connect to Anycast IPs, enter the AWS backbone near them, and are routed to the nearest healthy game server region, reducing jitter and inconsistent routing.

screens.title: CloudFront vs Global Accelerator
screens.narratorSegment: Distinguishing CloudFront and Global Accelerator is critical for correct design. CloudFront is a CDN: it caches static and semi-dynamic content at Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches, reducing origin load and speeding delivery for assets like images, videos, and script files. It also offers DDoS protections at the edge. Global Accelerator, by contrast, does not cache content; it provides static Anycast IPs and routes dynamic traffic through the AWS backbone to reach optimal endpoints, improving availability and consistent latency for interactive workloads. Use CloudFront when your primary goal is to offload and cache content and to accelerate large static payloads. Use Global Accelerator when your application requires a predictable, low-latency path for dynamic, session-based, or real-time traffic. You can combine them: CloudFront for static assets and Global Accelerator for A P I calls and real-time sessions. A common misconception is thinking Global Accelerator replaces CloudFront; it does not. Key takeaway: match CloudFront to caching problems and Global Accelerator to transport consistency problems. CloudFront vs Global Accelerator means use cloudfront for caching and shutdown of origin load; use global accelerator for consistent routing of dynamic, latency-sensitive traffic; combine when needed.. In practical terms, when to use each service, and when to use both. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › CloudFront vs Global Accelerator
CloudFront
Best for caching static and semi-dynamic content, reducing origin load, and serving large media files from the edge.
Use cases: websites, streaming media, API response caching.
Global Accelerator
Best for routing dynamic, interactive traffic via static Anycast IPs and the AWS backbone to reduce jitter and variability.
Use cases: gaming, VoIP, real-time feeds, APIs requiring consistent latency.
Combined pattern
Serve static assets via CloudFront and route interactive API calls through Global Accelerator so each layer does what it does best.

screens.title: Designing a Layered Global Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Design patterns matter. A layered architecture typically uses CloudFront for static assets, Global Accelerator for dynamic session traffic, and regional endpoints for backend processing. Start by mapping user geography and traffic types: static files go to CloudFront with cache-control suited to update frequency; A P I calls and WebSocket sessions can use Global Accelerator so clients connect via Anycast IPs and traverse the AWS backbone to regional load balancers. Backends remain in Regions and spread across AZs for resilience. This pattern reduces origin costs, improves perceived performance for static content, and reduces jitter for interactive calls. A common pitfall is over-caching personalized endpoints; use short-lived tokens or bypass caches for personalized data while caching shared assets aggressively. For testability, instrument both CloudFront headers and application latencies, and run tests from diverse geographies to validate improvements. Key takeaway: separate content and transport concerns—cache content at the edge and optimize transport for real-time traffic. Designing a Layered Global Architecture means layer edge caches, optimized transport, and regional endpoints so each layer focuses on either content delivery or reliable transport.. In practical terms, combine edge caching, regional endpoints, and optimized routing for real workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Layered Architecture
Layer roles
  • Edge: CloudFront caches static assets and serves global consumers.
  • Transport: Global Accelerator provides consistent routing for dynamic sessions.
  • Regional backends: Application services run in Regions across AZs for resilience.
Misconception
Treating a CDN as a transport optimizer. CDNs cache content; transport optimization comes from services like Global Accelerator.
Concrete scenario
An e-commerce platform uses CloudFront for assets and Global Accelerator for checkout APIs to ensure the checkout flow is low-latency and resilient across regions. Backends in each Region handle payments and inventory replication across AZs.
Key Takeaway
Design by responsibility: cache where content is stable, route where transport consistency matters.

screens.title: Configuring CloudFront for an S3 Static Website
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through the hands-on CloudFront and S3 activity so you can observe caching in action. Start by creating an S3 bucket configured for static website hosting and upload an index. html and an image. Make the objects public via a bucket policy that allows s3:GetObject for the bucket's contents. Then create a CloudFront distribution pointing to the S3 static website endpoint rather than the REST A P I endpoint; this preserves index document behavior. Choose Redirect HTTP to HTTPS and an appropriate cache policy like CachingOptimized. After the distribution deploys, test the distribution domain in a browser and inspect response headers. Expect the first request to be 'Miss from cloudfront' and later requests to show 'Hit from cloudfront' as the object becomes cached at the edge. A common mistake is selecting the S3 REST origin instead of the static website endpoint; that can change behavior for index documents. Key takeaway: observing X-Cache headers and testing from different regions validates that CloudFront effectively caches and accelerates your static content. screens.title: Use Cases and Decision Criteria
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right service is a decision guided by traffic characteristics. If you have heavy static assets like images, video, or JS libraries, CloudFront is the natural choice because it caches these items at the edge and reduces origin load. If your application handles interactive sessions—gameplay, VoIP, or real-time feeds—Global Accelerator provides the transport consistency and static IPs needed for low jitter and predictable routing. In many architectures both are appropriate: CloudFront serves static assets and Global Accelerator handles A P I calls or session-based traffic. Consider additional criteria: does your firewall or client configuration benefit from static Anycast IPs? Do you need the security benefits that CloudFront provides at the edge? Are your assets frequently changing such that caching becomes less beneficial? A common misconception is that Global Accelerator reduces bandwidth costs like a CDN; it does not—its benefit is in routing and availability. Takeaway: map your workload to the service that solves the primary pain point—content delivery versus transport optimization. Use Cases and Decision Criteria means pick cloudfront for caching large or stable assets; pick global accelerator for interactive, latency-sensitive traffic; use both when the application has both needs.. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to make global applications faster and more resilient by leveraging AWS's physical footprint: Regions, Availability Zones, and hundreds of Edge Locations. We'll link these building blocks to two services that optimize network performance: Amazon CloudFront for content delivery and AWS Global Accelerator for dynamic application traffic. You'll see why placing resources near users matters, how caching reduces origin load, and when Anycast IPs over the AWS backbone give consistently lower latency than the public internet. I will also show a practical pattern: CloudFront at the edge for static assets, and Global Accelerator for interactive A P I or session traffic. As we progress we'll examine a hands-on CloudFront configuration for an S3 static website so you can observe cache hits and misses. By the end you'll be able to pick the right service for images, APIs, or real-time streams and design a layered architecture that balances cost, performance, and resilience. Consider which part of your application most affects user experience: assets or interactive calls?

These objectives guide our lesson so you can apply AWS global infrastructure effectively. First, you will explain how Regions, Availability Zones, and Edge Locations affect latency and resilience; knowing this helps you place compute and storage close to users and reduces single points of failure. Second, you will describe AWS Global Accelerator: how it uses static Anycast IPs and the AWS backbone to route interactive traffic with lower variability than the public internet. Third, you will understand how Amazon CloudFront caches static and semi-dynamic content at Edge Locations to speed delivery and reduce origin load. Fourth, you will learn to choose between CloudFront and Global Accelerator and to design a basic layered global architecture combining both when appropriate. Each objective includes a short competency milestone so you can verify understanding by explaining a real architecture choice. Together these skills let you improve user experience for static content, A P I calls, and real-time sessions, and form the foundation for rigorous performance testing across geographies.

These applied objectives emphasize measurable skills you can demonstrate. You will interpret when CloudFront's caching policy will improve throughput for static assets and when cache-control headers matter for freshness. You will identify application patterns—such as gaming, VoIP, or real-time feeds—that benefit from Global Accelerator's Anycast IPs and backbone routing. You will plan an architecture that uses CloudFront for static distribution and Global Accelerator for dynamic A P I traffic, showing how the two can work together. Finally, you'll validate performance gains by testing from multiple locations and by reading CloudFront headers like X-Cache to confirm hits and misses. Each of these skills is practical: for example, spotting 'Miss from cloudfront' and knowing to tune cache policy or origin configuration is a sign of applied competency. These outcomes help you move from conceptual understanding to concrete, testable improvements that you can measure in latency, origin load, and user experience.

Start with the foundation: Regions and Availability Zones. A Region is a geographic area that contains multiple Availability Zones. An AZ is one or more discrete data centers with independent power, cooling, and networking, connected by low-latency links. Together, these define where your compute and storage run. The important performance rule is proximity: placing resources closer to your users reduces round-trip time. The important resilience rule is distribution: spreading instances across multiple AZs ensures that an outage in one AZ usually won’t fully take down your service. A common misconception is that Regions are a single data center; they are not. Another misconception is that AZ distribution alone solves global latency—if your users are on another continent, AZ distribution within one Region won't fix long-haul latency. A concrete example: serving a European user from an EU Region reduces latency compared to a US Region. When you design, map where users are, choose Regions closest to concentrations of traffic, and deploy across AZs in that Region for high availability. Key takeaway: placement controls both latency and fault isolation, so plan Regions for geographic reach and AZs for regional resilience.

Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches are the components that bring content physically closer to users. Edge Locations are numerous points of presence that serve cached content directly to end users. Regional Edge Caches sit between origins and Edge Locations, holding popular content for larger regions to reduce origin fetch frequency. The practical effect is twofold: latency is reduced because content often travels only to a nearby edge, and origin load decreases because repeated requests are served from edge caches. A common misconception is that caching only helps truly static files; in reality caching policies and invalidation allow CloudFront to serve semi-dynamic content when appropriate. For example, product images, C S S, and library files benefit hugely from edge caching, while frequently changing personalized data often should bypass caches or use short TTLs. When setting cache policies, consider object type, freshness requirements, and cache-control headers. Key takeaway: Edge Locations speed delivery and Regional Edge Caches amplify cache effectiveness across a region, together reducing latency and origin pressure. Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches means edge locations immediately serve cached content to reduce latency; regional edge caches act as regional staging layers to lower origin requests.. In practical terms, how amazon places content close to users and why that reduces origin load. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the request lifecycle for CloudFront so you can see how cache hits and misses affect latency and origin load. When a user requests an object, CloudFront first checks the nearest Edge Location. If the object is cached and valid, CloudFront returns it immediately — this is a cache hit and yields the lowest latency. If not cached, the request may be forwarded to a Regional Edge Cache; if it's present there, the response is returned and the Edge caches it for subsequent users. On a miss at both levels, CloudFront fetches the object from the origin, such as an S3 static website endpoint or an Application Load Balancer, and then caches it according to the distribution's cache policy. Important controls include Cache-Control headers, CloudFront cache policies, and invalidation requests which force removal of cached objects. A common misconception is that the first user always experiences the same latency as later users; in fact, the first request will often be slower due to origin fetch, while subsequent requests are faster because of cached copies. Takeaway: tune TTLs and origins to maximize hits for stable assets and plan for misses in load tests.

AWS Global Accelerator provides static Anycast IP addresses that act as fixed entry points for your users. When a client connects to one of these Anycast IPs, the connection is accepted at the nearest Edge Location. From there, Global Accelerator routes the traffic across the AWS backbone to the optimal healthy endpoint—this might be an Application Load Balancer or an EC2 instance in the best Region. The main benefit is consistent and often lower latency compared to routing over the public internet, because the majority of the path uses the optimized AWS network. A common misunderstanding is thinking Global Accelerator caches content; it does not. Instead, it optimizes transport for dynamic or interactive traffic where content changes frequently or sessions must persist. For instance, a multiplayer game uses Global Accelerator to direct a player to the nearest healthy game server with minimal jitter. When considering Global Accelerator, evaluate session patterns, whether static Anycast IPs simplify firewall rules, and whether your application gains from routing consistency. Key takeaway: Global Accelerator optimizes routing and availability—not caching—and is ideal for interactive, latency-sensitive workloads.

Distinguishing CloudFront and Global Accelerator is critical for correct design. CloudFront is a CDN: it caches static and semi-dynamic content at Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches, reducing origin load and speeding delivery for assets like images, videos, and script files. It also offers DDoS protections at the edge. Global Accelerator, by contrast, does not cache content; it provides static Anycast IPs and routes dynamic traffic through the AWS backbone to reach optimal endpoints, improving availability and consistent latency for interactive workloads. Use CloudFront when your primary goal is to offload and cache content and to accelerate large static payloads. Use Global Accelerator when your application requires a predictable, low-latency path for dynamic, session-based, or real-time traffic. You can combine them: CloudFront for static assets and Global Accelerator for A P I calls and real-time sessions. A common misconception is thinking Global Accelerator replaces CloudFront; it does not. Key takeaway: match CloudFront to caching problems and Global Accelerator to transport consistency problems. CloudFront vs Global Accelerator means use cloudfront for caching and shutdown of origin load; use global accelerator for consistent routing of dynamic, latency-sensitive traffic; combine when needed.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's summarize the essential concepts you should remember. First, an AWS Region is a geographic area that contains multiple Availability Zones, and AZs are the isolated data centers used to provide regional resilience. Second, Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches are the CDN backbone that bring cached content near users to reduce latency and take load off origins. Third, AWS Global Accelerator provides static Anycast IP addresses and routes traffic over the AWS backbone to optimal endpoints, improving the consistency of dynamic application performance. Each of these items plays a different role—placement and resilience, caching, and transport optimization. Keep these roles in mind when mapping application requirements to infrastructure choices. A quick self-check: can you identify whether your problem is primarily caching, regional placement, or transport variability? That answer guides the service selection.

A few final concise definitions will help cement what we've covered. AWS Global Accelerator supplies static Anycast IP addresses and routes traffic onto the AWS backbone toward the best healthy endpoint, improving availability and consistency for dynamic traffic. Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network that caches static or semi-dynamic content at Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches to reduce latency and origin load. Anycast IP is a routing approach where the same address is announced from many locations and traffic is delivered to the nearest or best instance, which is central to how Global Accelerator accepts connections at the edge. Keep these distinctions clear: CloudFront caches content, Global Accelerator routes transport efficiently, and Anycast provides global static entry points. Ask yourself: does my workload need faster content delivery, or does it need more predictable, low-latency transport? Your answer selects the right tool.
